title: Daffodil sprig in cross-stitch
subtitle: Two daffodil heads on a single stem on 14-count Aida
excerpt: A daffodil sprig is a 55-by-90 stitch piece on 14-count Aida. Two facing daffodil heads share a stem and use six floss colours: lemon, yellow, tangerine for the trumpet and petals, and two greens for the stem and leaves. Finished size is about 10 x 16 cm in a narrow hoop or frame.
sourceNotes: Original design for Homemade cross-stitch library. Daffodil motifs appear in British decorative arts traditions; the narcissus is documented in Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776.

content.text: A daffodil sprig is a 55-by-90 stitch piece on 14-count
colours cover the lemon petals, the deep orange trumpet, the pale petal undersides, and the two greens of stem and leaf. All full crosses except a
line on the thin stem section. The tall shape, about 10 x 16 cm, suits a slim frame or a 15 cm hoop on its narrowest axis.

items.name: 14-count Aida, white or cream
items.substitutions: Pale blue Aida gives a spring sky feel

content.text: Find the fabric centre. The chart centre falls between the two flower heads on the stem. Begin with the upper flower head, work the trumpet (741, 3820) first, then surround it with petals (3078, 3824).
Stitch the second flower head below. Because the heads face slightly different directions on the chart, check the petal directions carefully before placing the first stitches.
Stitch the stem and leaves (523 for the lighter face, 520 for shadow on the underside) working from the base of the lower head down to the bottom of the leaf shapes.
Add back-stitch in a single strand of 520 where the stem narrows between the flower base and the leaf attachment point.

Wash gently and press face-down until the stitches sit smooth and flat. The vertical shape suits a slim portrait frame. Pairs well as a diptych with the poppy-and-seed-head piece in a matching frame size.

items.symptom: The trumpet centre looks flat rather than cup-shaped
items.cause: The trumpet shading was worked in a single colour rather than using the darker tone at the rim.
items.fix: Use the deeper orange at the trumpet rim (the outer ring of chart squares) and the lighter yellow-gold inside. Once the rim colour is in, the cup depth reads clearly. Work the rim stitches first, then fill the centre until the contrast is visible.

items.symptom: The petals look too yellow compared with the finished image
items.cause: The petal colour is the pale primrose (745) but a warm yellow (307) was used instead.
items.fix: Check the floss label before threading: 745 is pale primrose, not a saturated yellow. Hold the thread against a white piece of paper in daylight to verify the undertone is cool rather than warm before stitching the petals.

content.text: The botanical fern frond in the same sub-category makes a good companion piece. It uses the same narrow vertical shape but in a green-only palette.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.
